1 Introduction

In today’s data-driven corporate environment, understanding customer behavior and effectively managing inventories are key to organizational success. With the increased availability of transactional, demographic, and behavioral data, data mining and clustering techniques—particularly K-Means clustering—have become critical decision-making tools in retail, logistics, and marketing. Recent studies emphasize that algorithm selection and data preprocessing directly affect the quality of insights derived from clustering (Prasetiya and Prayoga (2025)).

K-Means clustering is a machine learning technique that divides data into distinct clusters based on similarities, allowing businesses to identify patterns that would not be visible using traditional analysis. Research has demonstrated that it can greatly enhance consumer segmentation, inventory forecasting, and marketing optimization across various industries. For example, a weighted K-Means model produced more meaningful and stable customer clusters compared to the standard model (Omol et al. (2024)). Similarly, comparative work on the same dataset found that while more complex models can sometimes yield higher precision, K-Means remains valuable for its interpretability and speed in operational settings (Prasetiya and Prayoga (2025)).

In emerging markets, K-Means has also proven beneficial for small and resource-limited businesses. Clustering transactional and demographic data enables grocery stores to identify clear patterns of consumer purchasing behavior (Sitorus et al. (2023)). Likewise, studies show that clustering supports targeted marketing, loyalty programs, and more efficient stock management (Bala (2012)). Collectively, these works underscore that even small or localized retailers can leverage K-Means-based segmentation to align supply, demand, and promotional strategy.

Beyond retail, advances in clustering algorithms—including weighted variants (Omol et al. (2024)) as well as Global and MiniBatch K-Means—have improved computational efficiency and accuracy, reducing issues like random initialization and scalability on large datasets. These enhancements make K-Means increasingly suitable for real-time analytics and modern business intelligence frameworks. In summary, the literature shows that K-Means clustering is more than a statistical technique; it is a strategic enabler for data-informed decision-making. By uncovering relevant behavioral patterns in large datasets, firms can deepen customer understanding, optimize resource allocation, and forecast demand more accurately. Integrating K-Means into corporate analytics frameworks is thus a crucial step toward operational excellence and maintaining competitiveness in the digital economy.

1.1 Literature Review

Research shows that K-Means clustering is widely used in retail to improve customer segmentation and inventory forecasting. According to Prasetiya and Prayoga (2025), studies between 2019–2024 identified that combining K-Means with association rule learning (like FP-Growth) helps retailers better understand customer behavior and create focused marketing campaigns. The review also highlights that K-Means performs reliably on large datasets and can be applied to classify products by sales speed — such as fast-moving and slow-moving goods.

Omol et al. (2024) applied K-Means clustering to grocery stores in Kenya using transactional and demographic data. Their study showed that age and income strongly influence shopping behavior. Retailers could use this information to manage inventory and target marketing efforts more effectively.

Bala (2012) introduced a forecasting model combining clustering and demand prediction. This approach improved inventory accuracy, reduced excess stock, and minimized shortages — showing that clustering can make supply chains leaner and more efficient. Similarly, Sitorus et al. (2023) used K-Means to group products by demand at a retail store and identified three categories: fast, moderate, and slow sellers. This helped optimize stock levels and reduce costs.

Together, these studies demonstrate that K-Means clustering helps retailers improve both marketing precision and inventory control by identifying customer patterns and linking them to product demand. For example, clustering results can be used to align promotional strategies with inventory decisions, creating an integrated, data-driven retail management system (Prasetiya and Prayoga (2025); Omol et al. (2024); Bala (2012); Sitorus et al. (2023)).

2 Methods

This project applies the K-Means clustering algorithm to identify sales and inventory patterns within the (Montgomery County, Maryland, Government (2025)). The data contain monthly sales information by supplier, item code, and item type, allowing segmentation of products and suppliers into categories such as fast-, medium-, and slow-moving items. The overall workflow involves data preprocessing, feature engineering, determination of the optimal number of clusters, application of the K-Means algorithm, and interpretation of cluster characteristics relevant to inventory management.

2.1 Data Preparation

The dataset was obtained from (Montgomery County, Maryland, Government (2025)). It includes supplier names, item types, sales values, and dates (month, year).

Steps taken before analysis included:

  • Cleaning: Replacing missing supplier or item types with “Unknown” and filling null sales values with zero.

  • Feature Creation: Adding a TOTAL_SALES column by summing retail, transfer, and warehouse sales.

  • Date Formatting: Combining YEAR and MONTH into a single DATE field.

  • Aggregation: Summarizing data monthly by supplier and item code to create consistent records for clustering.

2.2 Feature Engineering

For each supplier or product, several key numerical features were calculated to represent inventory performance:

Feature Description
total_sales Total sales over the study period
avg_monthly Average monthly sales volume
std_monthly Standard deviation of monthly sales
cv_monthly Coefficient of variation (sales stability)
active_months Months with nonzero sales
warehouse_share Ratio of warehouse to total sales

These variables capture sales level, stability, and channel dependence. All values were standardized using z-score normalization for fair comparison.

2.3 Determining the Optimal Number of Clusters

Selecting an appropriate number of clusters K is crucial for meaningful segmentation. Three complementary techniques were used:

  1. Elbow Method: The Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) was plotted against increasing values of 𝐾. The point where the rate of improvement sharply declines (“the elbow”) suggests an optimal value.(MacQueen (1967))

\[ WCSS = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{x_i \in C_k} \| x_i - \mu_k \|^2 \]

  1. Silhouette Coefficient: Measures how well each observation fits within its assigned cluster versus neighboring clusters, ranging from -1 (poor) to +1 (well-separated).(Rousseeuw (1987))

\[ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i), b(i))} \]

  1. Practical Interpretation: K=3 was chosen for managerial relevance in order to represent the conventional fast-, medium-, and slow-moving inventory classifications frequently found in retail analytics.

2.4 K-Means Clustering Process

By reducing the overall within-cluster variance, the K-Means algorithm divides data into K clusters(Lloyd (1982)):

\[ \min_{C_1, \dots, C_K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{x_i \in C_k} \|x_i - \mu_k\|^2 \]

Algorithm steps:

  • Set up K centroids at random.

  • Using the Euclidean distance, assign each record to the closest centroid.

  • Centroids should be recalculated as the average of all allocated points.

  • Continue until the centroids stabilize.

2.5 Cluster Validation and Profiling

Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz indices were used to confirm cluster quality in order to guarantee separation and compactness. Segments were classified as fast, medium, or slow movers based on the median characteristics for each cluster (such as total sales, coefficient of variation, and warehouse share).

The analysis of supplier patterns and cluster differences was aided by visualizations including heatmaps, charts, and bar plots.

3 Data Exploration and Visualization

3.1 Data Sources and Collection:

The Montgomery County Maryland Open Data Portal(Montgomery County, Maryland, Government (2025)) provided the dataset used in the present study.

It includes comprehensive monthly records of alcohol sales from 2017 to 2020 that were gathered by the Department of Liquor Control from both retail locations and warehouse operations. Every record contains details regarding:

  • Supplier name (vendor providing the product)

  • item kind (beer, wine, spirits, etc.) and item code

  • Retail sales, retail transfers, and warehouse sales are a few such sales channels.

  • Temporal features: month and year

In order to encourage transparency in local government operations and business analytics research, the dataset is updated frequently and published under a Public Domain License.

3.2 Exploratory Analysis

The dataset was cleaned and summarized to look at overall sales trends, supplier performance, and product movement before the K-Means technique was applied. To comprehend central patterns and variability, descriptive statistics were produced using R Studio (tidyverse, ggplot2, and lubridate).

# Remove duplicate rows
data <- distinct(data)

# Handle missing values (replace or remove)
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    SUPPLIER = ifelse(is.na(SUPPLIER), "Unknown Supplier", SUPPLIER),
    `ITEM TYPE` = ifelse(is.na(`ITEM TYPE`), "Unknown Type", `ITEM TYPE`),
    `RETAIL SALES` = ifelse(is.na(`RETAIL SALES`), 0, `RETAIL SALES`),
    `RETAIL TRANSFERS` = ifelse(is.na(`RETAIL TRANSFERS`), 0, `RETAIL TRANSFERS`),
    `WAREHOUSE SALES` = ifelse(is.na(`WAREHOUSE SALES`), 0, `WAREHOUSE SALES`)
  )

# Create a Total Sales column
data <- data %>%
  mutate(TOTAL_SALES = `RETAIL SALES` + `RETAIL TRANSFERS` + `WAREHOUSE SALES`)

# Combine YEAR and MONTH into a proper Date column
data <- data %>%
  mutate(Date = make_date(YEAR, MONTH, 1))

# View first few cleaned rows in a table
head(data, 20) %>% 
  knitr::kable(caption = "first few Cleaned Retail Sales Data")

Code 
# Total Sales Trend Over Time

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)

# Ensure the Date column is in date format
data <- data %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date))

# Aggregate sales by date (if multiple transactions per day)
daily_sales <- data %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  summarise(Total_Sales = sum(TOTAL_SALES, na.rm = TRUE))

# Line chart for total sales trend
ggplot(daily_sales, aes(x = Date, y = Total_Sales)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "orange", size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Sales Trend Over Time",
    x = "Date of Transaction",
    y = "Total Daily Sales (in USD)"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "1 month") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
  )

Insights: This visualization shows the daily total sales trend over time. It highlights how sales fluctuate from day to day, revealing patterns such as peaks during high-demand periods and drops during slower days. The trend line helps identify overall performance changes and potential seasonal variations in sales.

For these major contributors, this pattern emphasizes the significance of keeping solid supplier relationships and precise demand forecasting.

Liquor and Wine occupy the second and third spots, reflecting moderate but sustained demand. The fact that categories like dunnage, kegs, and non-alcoholic items make up very little of the overall revenue highlights the fact that alcoholic beverages are the main driver of the county’s retail sector.

  • Beer’s dominance suggests a fast-moving inventory sector due to frequent use and high brand loyalty. However, goods classified as “Kegs” and “Non-Alcoholic” move slowly and would need focused marketing techniques to boost sales.
Code 
# Comparison: Retail vs Warehouse Sales

sales_compare <- data %>%
  summarise(
    Retail_Sales = sum(`RETAIL SALES`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Warehouse_Sales = sum(`WAREHOUSE SALES`, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Category", values_to = "Sales")

ggplot(sales_compare, aes(x = Category, y = Sales, fill = Category)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Retail vs Warehouse Sales", x = "", y = "Sales") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Insights:Warehouse sales are almost three times greater than retail sales, according to the analysis. This implies that rather than being sold directly to customers, the majority of merchandise is transferred in large quantities via centralized distribution. Although this type of layout promotes productivity, careful inventory balancing is necessary to prevent overstocking.

Code 
# Monthly Sales Heatmap
library(viridis)

monthly_sales <- data %>%
  group_by(YEAR, MONTH) %>%
  summarise(Total_Sales = sum(TOTAL_SALES, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(monthly_sales, aes(x = factor(MONTH), y = factor(YEAR), fill = Total_Sales)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis(option = "magma", direction = -1, labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Sales Heatmap", x = "Month", y = "Year", fill = "Total Sales") +
  theme_minimal()

Insights:Due to seasonal and holiday demand spikes, sales activity peaks between December and the middle of the year. Early months see lower sales, while anomalies in 2020 point to potential outside interruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Planning stock levels around seasonal trends is made easier by identifying these patterns.

4 Analysis and Results

4.1 Modeling and Data Preparation

In order to eliminate duplicates, fill in missing values, and normalize variables for analysis, the Montgomery County retail dataset performed preprocessing. Retail, warehouse, and transfer sales were combined to produce a new Total Sales feature that made sure every record represented all transaction activity. The important quantitative variables—Total Sales, Retail Sales, and Warehouse Sales—were then grouped based on their sales volume and consistency using K-Means clustering.

K = 3 was found to be the ideal number of clusters using the Elbow and Silhouette methods, creating three separate groups that represented Fast-Moving, Moderate-Moving, and Slow-Moving objects.

4.2 Cluster Formation and Categorization

Cluster Characteristics Interpretation
Cluster 1 – Slow-Moving Items Low total sales, high fluctuation, minimal retail movement Items with limited or irregular demand, including niche products and low-selling categories.
Cluster 2 – Fast-Moving Items Very high total and warehouse sales, stable demand Core items—especially beer and top liquor brands—requiring frequent replenishment.
Cluster 3 – Moderate-Moving Items Mid-range sales and steady monthly performance Consistent products such as wines and mid-tier liquors, showing predictable but moderate sales.

4.3 Visualization-Based Evidence

1.Top Suppliers by Total Sales: Crown Imports, Miller Brewing Company, and Anheuser Busch Inc. are the top contributors, according to the supplier study. Their products are part of the Fast-Moving cluster, which drives the majority of overall sales and reflects ongoing consumer demand. Depending on category performance, lower-end suppliers like The Wine Group and Jim Beam Brands Co. represent either Moderate-Moving or Slow-Moving inventories.

2.Total Sales by Item Type: Beer is clearly in the Fast-Moving category since it dominates overall sales. While categories like kegs, dunnage, and non-alcoholic items show minimal turnover and are categorized as Slow-Moving, wine maintains a robust but moderate flow—Moderate-Moving. This pattern demonstrates that the primary sources of income are alcoholic beverages.

3.Retail vs Warehouse Sales: Comparison Retail sales (~2.1 M) are much smaller than warehouse sales (~7.8 M). Most Fast-Moving products with high warehouse volumes are kept in bulk to satisfy steady demand. The Moderate or Slow-Moving clusters include items with little warehouse activity but sporadic retail transactions.

4.Heatmap of Monthly Sales: Fast-moving products that respond to event-driven consumption have seasonal maxima in the summer and December. Moderate-Moving products are those with consistent but reduced sales over the course of several months, whereas Slow-Moving clusters are those with inconsistent or occasional activity. The inconsistent 2020 data probably reflects market disturbances brought on by the epidemic.

4.4 Cluster Insights

  • Slow-Moving Items (Cluster 1): Specialty goods and low-demand categories, such as kegs or non-alcoholic items.  To increase turnover, they require tactics for reducing inventory and focused promotions.

  • Fast-Moving items (Cluster 2) :Include premium liquor, beer, and products from top suppliers with high warehousing and total sales. To avoid stock-outs, these need regular replenishing, precise forecasting, and ongoing observation.

  • Moderate-Moving Items (Cluster 3): These include secondary brands and mid-tier goods like wine. They keep sales consistent, which is perfect for managed safety stock and balanced reorder cycles.

5 Conclusion

5.1 Key Findings

  • The K-Means clustering divided the products into three clear groups — Fast-Moving, Moderate-Moving, and Slow-Moving items.

  • Fast-Moving items, like beer and popular liquor brands from suppliers such as Crown Imports and Miller Brewing, had very high and steady sales. These products need to be restocked often.

  • Moderate-Moving items, such as wine, showed average and regular sales. They are stable products that need balanced inventory levels.

  • Slow-Moving items had low or irregular sales, mostly niche or seasonal goods. These products need careful monitoring to avoid overstock and storage costs.

  • Sales increased during holiday seasons like summer and December, showing that demand changes with time and events.

5.2 Results Summary

The clustering results helped group inventory based on sales behavior and stock movement.

This makes it easier for managers to:

  • Focus on fast-selling items to keep shelves full,

  • Maintain enough stock of moderate-selling items, and

  • Reduce extra inventory of slow-selling items.

Using K-Means clustering for inventory helps stores plan better, avoid waste, and respond quickly to customer demand. Overall, it supports smarter inventory control, better forecasting, and more efficient retail operations.
